prompt.context: Your client is the division of a global consumer products company that produces toothbrushes. Its product portfolio consists primarily of a "manual" toothbrush that retails for $3 and an electric "rechargeable" toothbrush that retails for $50. One year ago, a new competitor introduced a battery-powered electric "spinbrush" that retails for $5 and now controls 1% of the worldwide toothbrush market. Your client currently lacks a comparable offering.
prompt.question: Should the client develop a spinbrush product similar to the competitor's offering?

clarifying_info.q: What was the market composition before the spinbrush launched?
clarifying_info.a: One year ago, the worldwide market was made up of 80% manual and 20% rechargeable toothbrushes.

clarifying_info.q: Where did the spinbrush's 1% market share come from?
clarifying_info.a: The spinbrush's 1% market share gain has come mostly at the expense of rechargeable toothbrush sales.

clarifying_info.q: What is the client's margin on manual toothbrushes?
clarifying_info.a: The client's net profit margin on sales of manual toothbrushes is 66%.

clarifying_info.q: How many manual toothbrushes does an average user buy per year?
clarifying_info.a: The average manual toothbrush user goes through 4 toothbrushes per year, of which 2 are given free by their dentist — so 2 are purchased.

clarifying_info.q: How are rechargeable toothbrushes structured and priced?
clarifying_info.a: Rechargeable toothbrushes are sold as two components: a base that retails for $50 (60% net profit margin) and a head that retails for $5 (90% net profit margin). 1 base and 1 head are needed at all times; no other components are compatible.

clarifying_info.q: What is the lifespan of a rechargeable base?
How many heads does a rechargeable user go through per year?
clarifying_info.a: The average rechargeable toothbrush user goes through 2 heads per year and purchases bases as needed.

clarifying_info.q: What are the production costs for a spinbrush?
clarifying_info.a: No specific cost data is known for the competitor's spinbrush. Client product development believes it could produce a spinbrush knockoff at a cost of $3 per brush.

exhibits.shows: A page from the casebook containing math analysis and the solution narrative — this is part of the answer key and should not be shown to the candidate upfront.

framework: Analyze profitability per customer per year for each product segment (manual, rechargeable, spinbrush)
Assess market share dynamics: which segment is threatened by the spinbrush
Evaluate strategic implications of launching a knockoff spinbrush
Consider alternative responses to the disruptive competitive threat
Form a recommendation on whether the client should enter the spinbrush segment

questions.prompt: Calculate the profit per customer per year for the manual toothbrush segment.
questions.guidance: Candidate should recognize that only 2 of the 4 annual toothbrushes are purchased (2 are given free by dentists). Apply the retail price and margin to the 2 purchased units.

questions.prompt: Calculate the profit per customer per year for the rechargeable toothbrush segment.
questions.guidance: Candidate must split into two components: heads (purchased annually) and base (purchased once per 10 years = 1/10 per year). Apply respective margins to each.

questions.prompt: Calculate the profit per customer per year for a spinbrush knockoff if the client were to launch one.
questions.guidance: No margin data is given directly; candidate should derive profit as (retail price − cost of production) × units purchased per year. Assume the same usage pattern as manual (2 purchased per year) since spinbrush is a $5 disposable-style product.

questions.prompt: Given the profitability analysis, what are the strategic implications of launching a spinbrush knockoff?
questions.guidance: Strong answer recognizes: (1) Manual and spinbrush generate the same $4/customer/year, so spinbrush is not incrementally profitable. (2) Rechargeable at $12/customer/year is far more valuable and is the segment losing share to the spinbrush. (3) Launching a knockoff spinbrush would likely accelerate cannibalization of the highly profitable rechargeable segment without compensating upside. The client should therefore NOT simply copy the competitor — it should explore alternative strategic responses.

brainstorming.prompt: What alternative strategies could the client use to respond to the spinbrush threat without launching a knockoff?

categories.name: Defend rechargeable segment
ideas: Improve rechargeable product features to increase perceived value vs. spinbrush
Lower price of rechargeable base to reduce barrier to entry
Introduce a premium rechargeable line to lock in loyal customers
Enhance marketing around rechargeable's superior cleaning effectiveness

categories.name: Attack the spinbrush market differently
ideas: Develop a differentiated (non-knockoff) battery toothbrush at a higher quality tier
Bundle spinbrush with rechargeable as an upsell/trial path
License competitor technology rather than develop internally

categories.name: Channel and distribution
ideas: Strengthen dentist partnerships to maintain free manual brush flow and steer patients toward rechargeable
Exclusive retail placements or promotions to crowd out competitor spinbrush shelf space

categories.name: Strategic M&A / partnership
ideas: Acquire the spinbrush competitor to control the segment
Form a co-branding partnership to neutralize the threat

recommendation: The client should NOT launch a spinbrush knockoff: it generates the same $4/customer/year as the manual product and would accelerate cannibalization of the far more profitable rechargeable segment ($12/customer/year).
Instead, the client should focus defensive investment on protecting and growing the rechargeable segment, which is the primary target of the spinbrush disruption.
risks: If the client does nothing, the spinbrush could continue to erode the rechargeable segment, permanently reducing the client's most profitable revenue stream.
A knockoff spinbrush could signal price competition and commoditize the mid-tier market, squeezing margins further.
next_steps: Quantify the total profit at risk from rechargeable share loss (requires knowing total market size and customer counts).
Evaluate specific rechargeable enhancement investments and their ROI.
Monitor spinbrush market share trajectory over the next 1-2 quarters to gauge rate of disruption.
